To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Drosophila Stoned proteins play an essential role in synaptic transmission by controlling the retrieval of Synpatotagmin I, which is required for synaptic vesicle endo–exo cycling.
Stoned proteins mediate SynaptotagmI retrieval and regulate synaptic transmission by controlling the endocytosis of synaptic vesicles.
stoned encodes two proteins that regulate synaptic vesicle endo–exo cycling by controlling the interaction of Synaptotagnim with the AP2 complex.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms that regulate the endocytosis of synaptic vesicles and the recycling of synaptic vesicle membrane proteins.
the mechanisms of synaptic vesicle endo- and exocytosis.
the molecular mechanisms underlying synaptic transmission.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Stoned proteins are involved in endocytotic retrieval of synaptic vesicles and that Synaptotgamin I is involved in exocytotic release of synaptic vesicles.
the Stoned/Synaptotagmin interaction is essential for synaptic vesicle endocytois and the regulation of synaptic transmission strength.
the Stoned protein family regulates the size of the synaptic vesicle pool in a Synaptotagmim I dependent manner.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Synaptotagemin I is a major regulator of the synaptic vesicle pool, which is controlled by the Stoned protein complex, which in turn interacts with the endocytosis machinery.
Synaptotagnim I and the Stoned proteins interact to control synaptic vesicle endocyosis.
the Stoned protein complex controls the size of the readily releasable synaptic vesicle pool by regulating the retrieval of Synatotagmin I.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Stoned protein complex is required for endocytosis and that Synaptotgamin I is the cargo of the Stoned complex.
the AP-2–synaptotagmin interaction is a critical step in endocytosis and that the Stoned A and B proteins regulate this interaction.
the AP-2 complex is a major determinant of synaptic vesicle recycling, and that Synaptotgamin I is a major determinant for AP-2 complex localization.
